title: Welcome and Introduction to Natural Language Processing
subject: Natural Language Processing
targetAudience: Postgraduate students beginning the AIML NLP course who want an overview of the syllabus, course philosophy, and expectations.
summary:
This opening session sets the stage for the entire NLP course. The instructor explains the course philosophy: building deep, bottom-up understanding of NLP algorithms matters far more than simply chaining together pre-built APIs. Whether you end up working with Large Language Models, Edge AI deployments, or autonomous agentic systems, a solid theoretical foundation will serve you across all of them.

Students are strongly encouraged to participate actively during lectures. Since most postgraduate students are already working professionals, sharing real-world experiences with NLP applications enriches the learning for the entire class.

The session also covers practical logistics: coding assignments span across all enrolled sections (no rigid section boundaries), and regular short breaks are built into the long Sunday afternoon sessions. These breaks double as hands-on coding windows, helping students immediately apply theoretical ideas through quick programming exercises right from the first week.
keyConcepts: Understand the course structure and how foundational topics connect to advanced GenAI applications.
Prioritise deep theoretical intuition over shallow API-level implementations.
Learn the standard procedures for project allocations and classroom discussion norms.
Appreciate the real-world value of understanding language structure at an algorithmic level.

pageTranscripts: Natural Language Processing Welcome and Introduction to Natural Language Processing 📅 Published: 2026-06-02 🎓 Level: postgraduate 👥 Audience: Postgraduate students beginning the AIML NLP course who want an overview of the syllabus, course philosophy, and expectations. Lecture Summary This opening session sets the stage for the entire NLP course. The instructor explains the course philosophy: building deep, bottom-up understanding of NLP algorithms matters far more than simply chaining together pre-built APIs. Whether you end up working with Large Language Models, Edge AI deployments, or autonomous agentic systems, a solid theoretical foundation will serve you across all of them.Students are strongly encouraged to participate actively during lectures. Since most postgraduate students are already working professionals, sharing real-world experiences with NLP applications enriches the learning for the entire class.The session also covers practical logistics: coding assignments span across all enrolled sections (no rigid section boundaries), and regular short breaks are built into the long Sunday afternoon sessions. These breaks double as hands-on coding windows, helping students immediately apply theoretical ideas through quick programming exercises right from the first week. Key Learning Objectives Understand the course structure and how foundational topics connect to advanced GenAI applications. Prioritise deep theoretical intuition over shallow API-level implementations. Learn the standard procedures for project allocations and classroom discussion norms. Appreciate the real-world value of understanding language structure at an algorithmic level. What is Natural Language Processing? Definition Natural Language Processing (NLP) is a branch of Artificial Intelligence that focuses on enabling machines to understand, analyze, and generate human language — in the same way human beings communicate with each other. Key Concept: NLP is not the same as LLMs (Large Language Models) or Agentic AI. LLMs are a part of NLP — they are one technology within the broader NLP landscape. NLP is an area of study, much like "computer networks" or "cloud computing" is an area — it encompasses multiple techniques, algorithms, and applications. At its core, NLP asks: Can we teach machines to speak our language instead of us learning theirs? Instead of humans writing code in Java, Python, or C++, we want to communicate with machines in natural language — English, Hindi, Marathi, or any human language — and have the machine interpret and act on that communication. The Ultimate Goal The dream of NLP has always been to make human–machine interaction as natural as human–human interaction. As of today, this dream is largely becoming reality: You can talk to Alexa, Siri, or Google Assistant and they respond like a human would. Search engines are far more efficient than they were a decade ago — they understand intent, not just keywords. Machines can read a newspaper and summarize it for you. Machine translation allows you to communicate across language barriers in real time. Code-generation agents (like GitHub Copilot) take natural language instructions and produce executable code. What NLP Draws From Building NLP applications requires borrowing from several disciplines: Linguistics — structure and grammar of languages Psycholinguistics — how humans process language cognitively Cognitive Science — models of mental representation Mathematics & Statistics — probability, linear algebra, optimization Computer Science — algorithms, data structures, machine learning, deep learning Artificial Intelligence \(\supset\) NLP \(\supset\) LLMs AI is the broad umbrella. Within AI sits NLP (alongside ML, DL, Computer Vision, etc.). Within NLP sit Large Language Models, Transformers, and Agentic AI systems. Why Study NLP? The Centrality of Language to Intelligence What makes human beings intelligent? One of the most accepted answers is: our ability to communicate effectively. When we say one person is "more intelligent" than another, we often mean they have more world knowledge, they understand complex situations better, and they can articulate their understanding clearly. Language is the medium through which this intelligence is expressed. Since Artificial Intelligence aims to replicate human intelligence, it follows naturally that language understanding must be at the heart of AI. Text is the Largest Data Repository As one student in the lecture correctly observed: text is the largest repository of human knowledge. Consider: Emails, news articles, research papers, legal documents, social media posts — all are text. Speech is almost always converted to text (via STT/ASR) before further processing. Even video understanding often relies on transcripts and captions. In every sector — finance, healthcare, e-commerce, education — there exists a vast corpus of textual data waiting to be leveraged. Industry Demand & Career Opportunities NLP is currently experiencing explosive growth, particularly in the LLM and Agentic AI space. The job market includes roles such as: NLP Engineer Prompt Engineer Conversational AI Engineer Data Scientist (NLP-focused) Computational Linguist AI Engineer Major companies — OpenAI, Anthropic (Claude), Google (Gemini), Microsoft, Meta — have built billion-dollar businesses around language models, all of which are fundamentally NLP systems. The "Garbage In, Garbage Out" Principle A machine is only as good as its training data. If you feed it high-quality input, you get high-quality output. This makes understanding NLP fundamentals critical — so you can design systems that are robust, fair, and trustworthy. Note: Even in the age of automated agents (Agentic AI), the human's role is to make intelligent calls — knowing which technique to apply, which model to use (SLM vs. LLM vs. nano model), and when a lightweight classical approach is better than a resource-intensive deep learning pipeline. A Brief History of NLP Understanding history is important because research progresses by identifying gaps in what has been done before. Every new breakthrough builds on the limitations of prior approaches. The Eras of NLP Rule-Based Era (1950s–1970s) ELIZA (1966): One of the earliest NLP systems, developed by Joseph Weizenbaum at MIT. It simulated a psychotherapist by pattern-matching user input against a set of rules. Interestingly, patients reported feeling comfortable interacting with it — an early demonstration that humans can form emotional connections with text-based systems. Turing Test (1950): Alan Turing proposed that if a human cannot distinguish between conversing with a machine and a human, the machine can be said to "think." Early Machine Translation: During the Cold War, rule-based translation between English and Russian was developed and proved useful despite limited compute. Limitation: Required hand-crafted rules; no training data or compute power available. Symbolic / Knowledge-Based Era (1970s–1980s) Context-Free Grammars (CFGs) and expert systems became popular. Systems encoded linguistic knowledge explicitly — e.g., grammar rules, lexicons. Limitation: Brittle; could not handle the variability and ambiguity of real language. Statistical NLP Era (1990s–2000s) Data-driven approaches emerged as digital text corpora became available. Probabilistic models: \(n\)-gram language models, Hidden Markov Models (HMMs), probabilistic context-free grammars (PCFGs). Limitation: Required labeled training data and extensive feature engineering. Machine Learning Era (2000s–2010s) Algorithms like SVM, Naïve Bayes, Decision Trees, and Maximum Entropy models. Still required manual feature engineering — a labor-intensive and domain-specific process. Limitation: Feature engineering was the bottleneck. Deep Learning Era (2013–2017) Word2Vec (2013, Mikolov et al.): Breakthrough in learning dense vector representations of words automatically — no manual feature engineering. Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), LSTMs, GRUs for sequence modeling. Limitation: Sequential processing was slow; difficulty capturing long-range dependencies. Transformer Era (2017–Present) "Attention Is All You Need" (Vaswani et al., 2017) introduced the Transformer architecture with the self-attention mechanism. Enabled parallel processing of sequences and effective modeling of long-range dependencies. Led to BERT (2018), GPT series, T5, and the modern LLM explosion. Agentic AI Era (Present) LLMs are used as reasoning engines within autonomous agent frameworks. Systems can plan, use tools, access APIs, retrieve information, and execute multi-step workflows. Current Challenge: Pragmatic understanding; emotional intelligence; reliability; cost efficiency. Note: A key insight: Not every application needs Agentic AI or LLMs. Using a massive transformer for a simple classification task is like "using a rocket to go to the market." The cost (in GPU hours, latency, and carbon footprint) must be justified by the ROI. Classical statistical/ML approaches remain relevant and are often the right choice for well-scoped problems. NLP Applications NLP applications are everywhere — wherever there is language, there is an NLP application. Below is a categorized overview. Core NLP Tasks Speech Recognition (STT)Converting spoken language to text. Modern systems (e.g., OpenAI Whisper) handle noisy environments and background cancellation effectively. Text-to-Speech (TTS)Converting text to natural-sounding speech. Can now mimic specific voices (raising deep-fake concerns). Machine TranslationTranslating text from one language to another. Critical for multilingual societies like India, where local language content is rich and valuable. Information Retrieval (IR)Searching for relevant documents or passages from a large corpus. Underpins search engines and RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) systems. Information Extraction (IE)Extracting structured information from unstructured text: named entities (persons, organizations, locations), relations between entities, and events. Text SummarizationAutomatically generating concise summaries of longer documents while preserving key information. Sentiment AnalysisDetermining the emotional tone or opinion expressed in text (positive, negative, neutral). Question AnsweringBuilding systems that can answer natural language questions — from FAQ bots to complex reasoning systems. Document ClassificationCategorizing documents into predefined classes — spam detection, topic labeling, genre identification. Spell & Grammar CheckingTools like Grammarly that correct spelling and grammar in real time. Emerging & Domain-Specific Applications Conversational AI: Chatbots that handle customer service, e-commerce, and healthcare triage. Dialogue Interface to Databases (NL2SQL): Users write natural language questions; the system translates them to SQL, queries the database, and returns results in natural language. Code Generation Agents: GitHub Copilot, Cursor, etc. — natural language \(\rightarrow\) code. Cyberbullying Detection: Identifying harmful content on social media platforms. Fake News Detection: Classifying misinformation and disinformation. Plagiarism Detection: Tools like QuillBot that compare text against large corpora. Healthcare: Diagnostic agents, medical record summarization, clinical NLP. Legal: Contract analysis, e-discovery, case law search. Example: Why is Information Extraction hard? Consider the word "Tata." It could refer to: A person: Ratan Tata An organization: Tata Group A foundation: Ratan Tata Foundation Disambiguating such cases requires understanding context — a non-trivial NLP challenge. NLP Tools & Libraries Commercial (Cloud) NLP APIs Table: Commercial NLP Platforms Provider Key NLP Capabilities Google Cloud NLP Pre-trained models for entity analysis, sentiment analysis, content classification, syntax analysis. Amazon Comprehend Entity recognition, relationship extraction, PII (Personally Identifiable Information) detection, sentiment analysis. Microsoft Azure AI Enterprise-grade NLP, strong in healthcare (Text Analytics for Health), conversational AI (Azure Bot Service). IBM Watson Text understanding, tone analysis, knowledge graph integration for enterprise applications. Open-Source NLP Libraries NLTK Natural Language Toolkit — the original, most established Python NLP library. Extremely lightweight; needs minimal compute resources. Supports multilingual processing — can do tokenization, stop-word removal, POS tagging for Hindi, Marathi, Tamil, Bengali, and many more. Includes corpora (WordNet, stopwords, etc.) and classic algorithms. Excellent for education and research due to its simplicity and transparency. Now also supports deep learning integrations. spaCy Industrial-strength NLP — designed for production use. Faster than NLTK for many tasks. Provides character-level position information (character offsets) alongside tokens — more granular metadata. POS tags include both the tag and a human-readable explanation (e.g., "NNP: proper singular noun"). Optimized primarily for English (though multi-language support is growing). Better for dependency parsing and named entity recognition pipelines. Hugging Face The ecosystem that democratized transformer models. transformers library: Thousands of pre-trained models (BERT, GPT, T5, LLaMA, etc.). datasets: Standardized access to NLP benchmark datasets. tokenizers: Fast tokenizer implementations (BPE, WordPiece, SentencePiece). Model Hub: Community-driven repository of fine-tuned models. Stanford CoreNLP Java-based toolkit from Stanford University. Provides a comprehensive pipeline: tokenization, POS tagging, NER, parsing, coreference resolution. Good for Java-based production environments. TextBlob A simplified wrapper around NLTK and Pattern. Extremely beginner-friendly — ideal for quick prototyping of sentiment analysis, POS tagging, and noun-phrase extraction. Note: NLTK vs. spaCy — When to use which? Use NLTK for multilingual tasks, education, research, and when you need maximum transparency and control. Use spaCy for production English pipelines, dependency parsing, and when you need speed and character-level metadata. The two are largely interchangeable — you can build a complete NLP pipeline with either. Text Preprocessing Before feeding text into any NLP model — classical or modern — raw text typically undergoes a series of preprocessing steps. These steps serve to reduce noise, normalize the text, and reduce the token count, which directly translates to cost savings in LLM-based systems. Caution: Preprocessing is application-dependent. You should not blindly apply all steps. For example: For grammar checking, you must not remove stop words. For information retrieval or text summarization, removing punctuation and stop words often helps. For sentiment analysis, keeping negation words ("not," "never") is critical. Tokenization Tokenization is the process of splitting a larger chunk of text into smaller units called tokens. Tokens can be: Sentences — sentence tokenization Words — word tokenization Subwords — subword tokenization (BPE, WordPiece, SentencePiece) Example: Sentence Tokenization (NLTK): from nltk.tokenize import sent_tokenize text = "Hello all, I'm Dr. Chetana. Welcome to the lab session!" sentences = sent_tokenize(text) # ['Hello all, I'm Dr. Chetana.', # 'Welcome to the lab session!'] Word Tokenization (NLTK): from nltk.tokenize import word_tokenize tokens = word_tokenize("Hello all, I'm Dr. Chetana.") # ['Hello', 'all', ',', 'I', "'m", 'Dr.', 'Chetana', '.'] Notice that NLTK correctly distinguishes "Dr." (with the period as part of the abbreviation) from a sentence-ending period. This is non-trivial behavior. Advanced Tokenization Techniques The simple whitespace/punctuation-based tokenizer shown above is not what modern LLMs use. Advanced subword tokenization methods break words into meaningful subunits: BPEByte-Pair Encoding (used by GPT models). Starts with characters, iteratively merges the most frequent pairs. WordPieceUsed by BERT. Similar to BPE but merges based on likelihood rather than frequency. SentencePieceLanguage-agnostic; treats the input as a raw stream of characters (used by T5, LLaMA). Key Concept: Why do tokenization techniques matter so much? Token cost is directly tied to the number of tokens. When you use commercial APIs (OpenAI, Anthropic), you pay per token. A better tokenizer can represent the same text with fewer tokens — so an improved tokenization scheme, like the one DeepSeek introduced, can make an LLM both faster and computationally cheaper. Stop Word Removal Stop words are common words that carry little semantic significance in many NLP tasks. Examples: "the," "is," "at," "which," "on," "a," "an." from nltk.corpus import stopwords stop_words = set(stopwords.words('english')) text = "I am going to the market." filtered = [w for w in word_tokenize(text) if w.lower() not in stop_words] # ['I', 'going', 'market', '.'] Note: Domain-Specific Stop Words: You can (and should) customize the stop-word list for your domain. In bioinformatics, gene names or common lab terms might be stop words. In finance, domain-specific boilerplate terms can be filtered. NLTK supports stop-word lists for Indian languages (Hindi, Marathi, Tamil, Bengali, etc.) as well as major world languages. Lemmatization & Stemming Both techniques aim to reduce a word to its base/root form, thereby collapsing morphological variants into a single representation. This reduces vocabulary size and helps models generalize better. Stemming Stemming uses a set of heuristic rules to strip suffixes. It does not consult a dictionary — it is purely algorithmic. Porter Stemmer: The most widely used. Applies a sequence of rule-based transformations (e.g., "-ing" \(\to\) "", "-ational" \(\to\) "-ate"). Snowball Stemmer: An improved, multi-language version of Porter. Lancaster Stemmer: More aggressive; produces shorter stems but may over-stem. Regex Stemmer: User-defined regular expression rules. Example: Stemming in action: "running" \(\to\) "run" "happily" \(\to\) "happili" (note: not a real word — stems need not be valid words) "friendship" \(\to\) "friend" "natural" \(\to\) "natur" (Porter stemmer strips "-al") Lemmatization Lemmatization uses a dictionary (lexicon) to find the canonical form (lemma) of a word. It considers the word's part of speech and meaning before stripping. Requires a lexical resource like WordNet. Produces valid dictionary words. Can be guided by a domain dictionary — you specify which terms should be kept intact. Example: Lemmatization vs. Stemming: Word Stemming (Porter) Lemmatization running run running better better good studies studi study processing process processing natural natur natural Notice that lemmatization may retain suffixes if the domain dictionary says so (e.g., "processing" kept as-is in an NLP course context). Table: Stemming vs. Lemmatization Aspect Stemming Lemmatization Method Rule-based (algorithmic) Dictionary-based (lexicon lookup) Speed Fast Slower (needs dictionary) Output May not be a real word Always a valid word Domain knowledge None needed Can incorporate domain dictionary Accuracy Can over/under-stem More accurate, meaning-preserving Key Concept: The same idea behind stemming and lemmatization — breaking words into sub-word units — underlies modern subword tokenization (BPE, WordPiece). Just as "interest" \(+\) "ing" can be stored as two embeddings to cover "interesting," "interested," and "interests," BPE tokenizers split words into frequent subword units that can be recombined flexibly. POS Tagging (Part-of-Speech Tagging) POS tagging assigns each word a grammatical category: noun, verb, adjective, adverb, etc. import nltk tokens = nltk.word_tokenize("Dr. Chetana teaches NLP at BITS.") tags = nltk.pos_tag(tokens) # [('Dr.', 'NNP'), ('Chetana', 'NNP'), ('teaches', 'VBZ'), # ('NLP', 'NNP'), ('at', 'IN'), ('BITS', 'NNP'), ('.', '.')] Note: POS tagging is particularly useful for Named Entity Recognition (NER). Named entities (persons, organizations, locations) are typically proper nouns (NNP) or common nouns (NN) — they will never be adjectives or adverbs. POS tagging thus serves as a filtering step for NER pipelines and relationship extraction. The Challenge of Language Why is Language Hard for Machines? Despite being trivial for humans, language understanding is extraordinarily difficult for machines. Consider this simple four-line dialogue from a movie ticket booking scenario: User: I want to watch Black Panther. Where is it playing in Mountain View? System: Black Panther is playing at Century 16, Mountain View. User: When is it playing there? System: Showtimes are 2:00 PM, 5:30 PM, and 9:00 PM. User: Book me for the first show — one adult and two children. System: That will be $42.50. Confirming: 2:00 PM, 1 adult, 2 children at Century 16. What the Machine Must Do (Behind the Scenes) Entity Recognition: "Black Panther" \(\to\) movie name; "Mountain View" \(\to\) location (not a literal mountain view); "Century 16" \(\to\) theater name. Coreference Resolution: "it" \(\to\) Black Panther; "there" \(\to\) Century 16; "first show" \(\to\) 2:00 PM. Intent Understanding: "Book me" \(\to\) purchase tickets; "one adult and two children" \(\to\) ticket types and quantities. External API Calls: Check availability, fetch pricing, apply age restrictions, compute total cost. Response Generation: Synthesize a coherent, natural-language confirmation. All of this must happen in milliseconds for the interaction to feel natural. Types of Ambiguity in Language Ambiguity is the central challenge of NLP. Human language is filled with it at every level. Structural Ambiguity The same sequence of words can correspond to multiple syntactic structures, leading to different meanings. Example: Example 1 — Word Order Matters: \begin{align*} \text{Sentence A: } &\text{``Namrata thinks she understands me.''} \\ \text{Sentence B: } &\text{``She thinks Namrata understands me.''} \end{align*} In a Bag-of-Words model, both sentences are identical (same set of words). But their meanings are completely different — in A, Namrata is the subject; in B, Namrata is the object. The order of words carries meaning. Example: Example 2 — Two Parse Trees: "Visiting relatives can be a nuisance." This sentence has two interpretations: Visiting (verb) + relatives (object): The act of visiting one's relatives is a nuisance. Visiting relatives (compound noun): Relatives who are visiting you are a nuisance. If "visiting relatives" is parsed as a gerund phrase (verb + object), you get meaning 1. If parsed as a compound noun (adjective + noun), you get meaning 2. Humans disambiguate effortlessly via context; machines need explicit mechanisms. Grammatical (Morpho-Syntactic) Ambiguity English, in particular, has grammatical ambiguities that many other languages do not. Example: Gender Ambiguity: "I go now." In English, you cannot tell the gender of the speaker. But in Hindi or Marathi: "Main jaata hoon" \(\to\) male speaker "Main jaati hoon" \(\to\) female speaker Machine translation from English to a gender-marked language requires resolving this ambiguity — a non-trivial problem. Lexical Ambiguity (Word Sense Disambiguation) The same word can have multiple meanings depending on context. The same word can even have multiple parts of speech. Example: The word "can": Noun: "a can of milk" (container) Modal verb: "Can I go?" (permission/ability) Verb: "to can food" (to preserve in a can) The word "bank": Financial institution: "I deposited money in the bank." River bank: "We sat on the bank of the Ganga." Key Concept: This is precisely why contextual word embeddings (Word2Vec \(\to\) ELMo \(\to\) BERT \(\to\) GPT) were a breakthrough. Static embeddings (like early Word2Vec) assigned a single vector to "bank," conflating all its meanings. Contextual embeddings assign different vectors to "bank" depending on surrounding words — capturing the correct sense. Cultural & Temporal Ambiguity Language evolves. Words change meaning over time and across cultures. Example: The word "cool": 1980s/90s: "That's cool" \(\to\) That's interesting/nice (positive). Earlier usage: "He's a cool person" \(\to\) He's emotionally distant (negative). Gen Z usage: Sarcastic "cool" can mean the exact opposite depending on tone and context. Other Challenges New words: "Tandoori," "yoga," "selfie" — constantly being added to dictionaries. Emoticons and emojis: ":)" vs. sarcastic ":))" carry different meanings. Gen Z jargon: "no cap," "slay," "bet" — context-dependent and rapidly evolving. Exceptions to rules: "i before e except after c" — and then there's "science," "weird," "their" \(\ldots\) Tone of voice: The same words spoken in an angry tone vs. a calm tone convey entirely different meanings. Facial expressions and gestures: In face-to-face communication, much of the meaning is non-verbal. Note: Machines today can understand language at the word and sentence level, but they are not yet emotionally intelligent. They cannot reliably detect sarcasm, read between the lines, or interpret the complex interplay of tone, gesture, and context that humans use naturally. Levels of Language Understanding When humans process language, multiple layers of analysis happen simultaneously and automatically — we are not consciously aware of them. NLP systems attempt to replicate these layers explicitly. The layers are hierarchical: higher layers assume lower layers are already processed. Discourse (multi-sentence coherence, coreference) \(\uparrow\) Pragmatic (world knowledge, intent, situational context) \(\uparrow\) Semantic (meaning of words and sentences) \(\uparrow\) Syntactic (grammar, sentence structure) \(\uparrow\) Lexical (which affixes go with which roots) \(\uparrow\) Morphological (roots, prefixes, suffixes) Figure: The Language Understanding Pyramid Morphological Level Morphology is the study of how words are formed from smaller units called morphemes — the smallest meaning-bearing units of language. Root/Stem: The core meaning-carrying part. E.g., "teach" in "teacher," "teaching," "teaches." Prefix: Added before the root. E.g., "un-" in "undo," "pre-" in "preview." Suffix: Added after the root. E.g., "-er" in "teacher," "-ing" in "teaching." Infix: Inserted inside the root (rare in English, common in some languages). Example: Morphological decomposition: \begin{align*} \text{``unhappiness''} &= \underbrace{\text{un}}_{\text{prefix}} + \underbrace{\text{happy}}_{\text{root}} + \underbrace{\text{ness}}_{\text{suffix}} \\ \text{``biology''} &= \underbrace{\text{bio}}_{\text{root (life)}} + \underbrace{\text{logy}}_{\text{suffix (study of)}} \\ \text{``bioinformatics''} &= \text{bio} + \text{informatics} \end{align*} If you know "bio" = life and "logy" = study of, you can infer that "biology" = study of life — even if you have never seen the word before. This is exactly what subword tokenization (BPE) tries to leverage. Lexical Level At the lexical level, we know which affixes can attach to which roots. This is learned over years of language exposure. Example: Lexical knowledge in action: "friend" + "ship" = "friendship" correct "friend" + "ful" = "friendful" incorrect (it's "friendly") "beauty" + "ful" = "beautiful" correct "beauty" + "ship" = "beautyship" incorrect There is no general rule — you just know which combinations are valid. Your neural network (brain) has learned these associations through exposure. Syntactic Level Syntax is the set of rules that govern sentence structure — the grammar of a language. English: SVO (Subject–Verb–Object) — "I eat mango." Hindi/Marathi: SOV (Subject–Object–Verb) — "Main aam khata hoon" (I mango eat). Japanese/Korean: SOV, with topic markers. If you scramble the word order, the sentence becomes incomprehensible: "Mango I eat" \(\to\) understandable but awkward. "Eat I mango" \(\to\) confusing. "Mango eat I" \(\to\) nearly incomprehensible. Syntax enables us to distinguish "Dog bites man" from "Man bites dog" — the same words, different meanings, determined purely by structure. Semantic Level Semantics deals with meaning. A sentence can be syntactically perfect but semantically nonsensical. Example: Noam Chomsky's classic example: "Colorless green ideas sleep furiously." This sentence is grammatically flawless (Adj + Adj + N + V + Adv — a perfectly valid English structure). But it is semantically meaningless: ideas cannot be green or colorless; ideas do not sleep; nothing can sleep furiously. Yet a human instantly recognizes it as nonsense. A machine, without semantic understanding, might process it as just another valid sentence. Semantic analysis is where the heavy lifting of modern NLP happens: Word embeddings (Word2Vec, GloVe): Map words to dense vectors where similar meanings are close in vector space. Contextual embeddings (BERT, GPT): The same word gets different vectors depending on surrounding context — resolving the "bank" ambiguity discussed earlier. Attention mechanisms: Allow the model to focus on relevant parts of the input when computing meaning. Pragmatic Level Pragmatics goes beyond literal meaning to consider world knowledge, intent, and situational context. A statement can be semantically true but pragmatically wrong. Example: Semantic vs. Pragmatic: Semantically correct: "I cut the banana with a pen." Pragmatically incorrect: You don't cut bananas with pens — you use a knife. This violates world knowledge. Key Concept: In the Agentic AI paradigm, pragmatic understanding maps to: Episodic memory: Remembering past interactions and outcomes. Semantic memory: General world knowledge (what a knife is, what it's used for). Goal-awareness: Understanding what the user is trying to achieve, not just what they literally said. We are still struggling at the pragmatic level in current AI systems — this is an active area of research. Discourse Level Discourse concerns how sentences connect to form coherent text. It involves: Coreference Resolution: Identifying which words refer to the same entity. E.g., "Jane told Mary that she passed the exam." — Who does "she" refer to? Coherence: Ensuring the text flows logically from one sentence to the next. Discourse relations: Cause–effect, contrast, elaboration, etc. Example: Cross-sentence discourse: "Once upon a time, there lived a king and a queen in a beautiful kingdom. They ruled wisely and were loved by all. They lived happily together." "They" in the second and third sentences refers back to "the king and queen" — even though the explicit mention was two sentences ago. This is discourse-level coreference. Modern LLMs handle this via their context window (e.g., 128K tokens in GPT-4 Turbo), which allows them to "remember" earlier parts of the text. NLP System Architecture Every NLP system — whether a question-answering bot, a machine translation engine, or a text summarizer — has two fundamental components: Understanding (Analysis): Parse and interpret the input. Generation (Synthesis): Produce a coherent, appropriate output. Both components require: grammar/spelling knowledge, domain knowledge, and application-specific knowledge. Classical NLP Pipeline In the classical (pre-deep-learning) approach, each level of language understanding was implemented as a distinct module: \[ \text{Input} \to \underbrace{\text{Morphological Analysis}}_{\text{tokenization, stemming}} \to \underbrace{\text{Syntactic Analysis}}_{\text{POS tagging, parsing}} \to \underbrace{\text{Semantic Analysis}}_{\text{meaning extraction}} \to \underbrace{\text{Pragmatic Analysis}}_{\text{intent, context}} \to \text{Output} \] Advantages: Fully explainable, debuggable, no hallucinations, lightweight. Disadvantages: Requires extensive manual engineering; each module's errors propagate downstream. Modern (End-to-End) NLP Pipeline Modern systems use a transformer-based architecture where syntax and semantics are learned implicitly: \[ \text{Input} \to \underbrace{\text{Tokenizer}}_{\text{BPE/WordPiece}} \to \underbrace{\text{Transformer Encoder/Decoder}}_{\text{implicit syntax + semantics}} \to \underbrace{\text{Generation Head}}_{\text{produce output tokens}} \to \text{Output} \] Advantages: No manual feature engineering; state-of-the-art results on most benchmarks. Disadvantages: Black-box (not explainable); requires expensive GPUs; can hallucinate; billions of parameters. Hybrid NLP Pipeline (Production Standard) In practice, most production-ready systems use a hybrid approach: \[ \text{Input} \to \underbrace{\text{Lightweight Classical Preprocessing}}_{\text{tokenization, stop words, normalization}} \to \underbrace{\text{LLM / Transformer}}_{\text{understanding + generation}} \to \underbrace{\text{Classical Post-processing}}_{\text{validation, formatting}} \to \text{Output} \] Key Concept: Why hybrid? Transformers need GPUs. GPUs cost lakhs of rupees (an NVIDIA A100 can cost $10K–$15K; an H100 even more). For a startup or a cost-sensitive application, using a GPU for basic tasks like tokenization or stop-word removal is wasteful. Do the lightweight work with classical methods (NLTK/spaCy), and reserve the transformer for what it does best: deep semantic understanding and fluent generation. Evaluating NLP Systems Evaluation is critical. A client will not accept an NLP system that hallucinates, produces biased outputs, or fails on edge cases. Good evaluation tells you when your system works, when it fails, and why. Key Evaluation Criteria AccuracyThe most basic metric: fraction of correct predictions. Limitation: misleading for imbalanced datasets (e.g., 99% of emails are not spam — a model that always predicts "not spam" is 99% accurate but useless). FairnessThe system must not exhibit biases based on gender, race, caste, religion, etc. Since models learn from human-generated data, they can (and do) amplify societal biases. Garbage In, Garbage Out. ReliabilityThe system must produce consistent results. This is extremely difficult with large neural models (145B+ parameters) — identifying the root cause of a specific failure is challenging. This lack of explainability drives the push for AI governance. RobustnessThe system must generalize to diverse, unseen data. Overfitting to the training distribution is a failure mode. EfficiencyROI (Return on Investment): If a system costs Rs. 1 crore to deploy (GPUs, infrastructure, development), you expect at least Rs. 2 crores in returns. Latency: Users will abandon a system that takes minutes to respond — the "time to first token" must be low. UsabilityThe output must be fluent, coherent, and actionable by the end user. Common Evaluation Metrics Table: NLP Evaluation Metrics by Task Metric Primary Use Description Accuracy Classification \(\frac{\text{Correct predictions}}{\text{Total predictions}}\); good for balanced datasets. Precision IR, IE, Detection \(\frac{TP}{TP + FP}\); of all predicted positives, how many are actually positive? Recall Medical, Fraud \(\frac{TP}{TP + FN}\); of all actual positives, how many did we catch? F1 Score General Harmonic mean of Precision and Recall. BLEU Machine Translation Measures \(n\)-gram overlap between generated and reference translation. ROUGE Summarization Recall-oriented; measures \(n\)-gram overlap with reference summary. Perplexity Language Modeling Measures how "surprised" the model is by the test data. Lower = better. Why Precision and Recall Matter: A Medical Example Example: Cancer Detection — Both Errors Are Dangerous: False Positive (FP): The model predicts cancer when the patient is healthy. Consequence: Unnecessary mental trauma, invasive follow-up tests, costs. You want high precision: minimize false positives. False Negative (FN): The model predicts healthy when the patient has cancer. Consequence: Missed early treatment window; can cost a life. You want high recall: minimize false negatives. There is always a precision–recall trade-off. The right balance depends on the application and its tolerance for each type of error. The Explainability–Performance Trade-off Classical Models (Naïve Bayes, Decision Trees, SVM) \(\to\) High explainability, moderate performance, zero hallucination, low compute. Hybrid Systems (Classical preprocessing + LLM) \(\to\) Balanced: explainable pipeline with powerful generation. Pure LLM / Transformer (GPT-4, Claude, Gemini) \(\to\) High performance, low explainability, risk of hallucination, high compute cost. Note: The Black Box Problem: When a transformer with 175 billion parameters produces a wrong output, you cannot easily trace why. You cannot "debug" it in the traditional sense. This is a fundamental challenge for enterprise adoption, especially in regulated industries (finance, healthcare, law). Key Takeaways Summary of Lecture 1 NLP is a branch of AI that enables machines to understand, analyze, and generate human language. It is a broad field, not a single technology. The history of NLP shows a progression: Rule-based \(\to\) Symbolic \(\to\) Statistical \(\to\) ML \(\to\) Deep Learning \(\to\) Transformers \(\to\) Agentic AI. Each era built on the limitations of the previous one. Language is fundamentally ambiguous at every level — morphological, lexical, syntactic, semantic, pragmatic, and discourse. Resolving these ambiguities is the central challenge of NLP. Text preprocessing (tokenization, stop-word removal, lemmatization/stemming, POS tagging) is critical for reducing noise, saving compute, and improving downstream performance — even in the age of LLMs. NLTK and spaCy are the two dominant open-source NLP libraries. NLTK excels at multilingual tasks and education; spaCy excels at production English pipelines. Hybrid architectures (classical preprocessing + transformer-based core) are the production standard because they balance cost, explainability, and performance. Evaluating NLP systems requires more than accuracy. Fairness, reliability, robustness, efficiency, and usability are equally important. The choice of metric (accuracy vs. F1 vs. BLEU vs. ROUGE vs. perplexity) depends on the task. "Wisdom is not in words; wisdom is meaning within the words." — Khalil Gibran. This quote encapsulates why contextual embeddings were a breakthrough: they capture meaning, not just surface form.
